transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. Don’t test the magnetron or any internal microwave parts. Stop there: the high-voltage capacitor can retain a lethal charge even when the microwave is unplugged, and the cover must be fully refitted with all its screws before the appliance is used again. Because it runs with the light, fan and turntable working but does not heat, the likely fault is in the high-voltage heating circuit. That can be the magnetron, or—depending on the design—an inverter module or conventional high-voltage diode/capacitor/transformer. It cannot be safely narrowed down by DIY internal testing. The only useful owner checks are:
1. With the cover fully back on, use a microwave-safe cup containing water. Select a timed cook on full microwave power—not defrost, grill or combination—and run it for one minute. If the water is still cold, this suggests an internal heating-circuit fault.
2. Check the door closes firmly and clicks shut, with no food debris around the latch area. If it is loose or behaves differently when the door is pressed, an interlock fault is possible instead. If the water stays cold on full power and the door latches normally, arrange a microwave engineer or consider replacement depending on its age and repair quote.
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.

Did the water test, 1 min on full power and the water stayed cold. Door shuts fine too. I haven't discharged any capacitor, don't really know what that is tbh. It's unplugged now with the cover screws still out. Is it worth repairing, it cost about £100 new?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. At a £100 purchase price, it is usually not economical to pay for a microwave repair unless it is fairly new, under warranty, or you can get a very modest fixed-price quote. Diagnosis, labour and a high-voltage part can easily approach or exceed the cost of a replacement. The water test and normal door closure make this a high-voltage heating-circuit fault rather than a setting or basic door-latch issue. The failed item could be the magnetron, an inverter module, or—on a conventional design—the diode, capacitor or transformer; it cannot be identified safely without an engineer’s test. Do not use it or leave it with the casing loose: refit the cover and every original screw before it is moved on, repaired or disposed of. Do not attempt to discharge or test anything inside. If you want to pursue repair, obtain a diagnostic/fixed-price quote first and set a ceiling well below replacement cost. Otherwise, replacement is the sensible option. The exact model number from the rating label can help establish the type of heating system and whether a quote is worthwhile.
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.

Low power/defrost or incorrect cooking mode (medium)
